transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-22
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (RapidSprocket CTO), Priya Nair (Platform Engineer), Hana Alvarez (Product), Devon Park (Infra)

AUTO-GEN SUMMARY (may be rough):
RapidSprocket is evaluating Redwood for embedding and generation endpoints in a freemium to paid PLG flow. Primary asks: how fast they can get a prototype working, cost expected for low volume, security posture for regulated customers, and options for dedicated/private when they scale.

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, and with me is Maya, our solutions engineer. Quick sound check?
00:08 Liam (RapidSprocket CTO): Sounds good, can hear you.
00:10 Priya (RapidSprocket): Yep good here.
00:13 Jordan: Great. High level today — we want to understand your time horizon for a prototype, what success looks like, any hard constraints (data residency, compliance), and then walk through the quickest path using our hosted API versus when dedicated or private would make sense.
00:29 Liam: Perfect. We're trying to add a generative assistant in the product — start with a subset of customers. PLG motion, so fastest path to something in our staging env matters a lot. We also have a handful of enterprise prospects that will require data residency in EU and KMS integration down the road.
00:45 Maya (Redwood SE): Cool, thanks. Can you give a sense of your current stack and traffic profile? Even ballpark qps, avg tokens per request, that kind of thing.
00:53 Priya: We're on GCP, mostly Node/Go backends. For the prototype, expecting 50–150 requests/day, average 120 tokens generation per call. Peak for early alpha maybe 10 req/s but sustained lower.
01:10 Hana (Product): Success metric is basically shipping a feature in 2–3 weeks that product teams can demo. Latency under 500ms 95th for generation would be nice but not blocking — more concerned with developer experience and predictable cost early on.
01:25 Jordan: Got it. For that profile, hosted API is the fastest path — self-serve, free credits, SDKs. We'll talk numbers on credits but our standard PLG pack covers this sort of prototyping. If you want, we can provision credits and a sample repo that shows a serverless integration.
01:40 Liam: That sounds good. Two questions up front — first, how long from signup to first successful call? Second, if we outgrow the hosted plan, what's the migration path to dedicated?
01:51 Maya: First call is usually minutes after signup if you use the SDK or Postman collection; time-to-first-token depends on latency to your region and model chosen but for typical open models it's sub-second token streaming most of the time. Migration path: we support dedicated reserved capacity and private VPC installs; you can pin model versions and roll traffic — we help with data migration and testing.
02:12 Devon (Infra): On the private/VPC option, can you outline the KMS story? We need to know if customer-managed keys are supported for the private deployment, and whether audit logs go to our SIEM.
02:25 Maya: For Private we support customer-managed keys (KMS) and can push audit logs to an S3/Cloud Storage bucket or push via syslog to your SIEM. For Hosted we encrypt at rest and in transit; we offer envelope encryption and are SOC2. We'll send the exact SOC2 report stub and the KMS integration guide after this call.
02:45 Priya: That helps. Any gotchas on SDKs? We do most things server-side in Go.
02:52 Jordan: We have Go and Node SDKs, plus a plain REST interface. We also provide a lightweight Postman collection and sample serverless function. Coding-wise it's usually five to ten lines to initialize and send a request.
03:05 Liam: Cool. Can you share a realistic estimate of cost for our prototype — say 10k tokens/day?
03:12 Jordan: Rough numbers: for hosted API with open quantized models, unit cost per 1k tokens might be in the low cents range — I'll include exact tiers in the follow-up. For the 10k tokens/day example that's ballpark tens to a couple hundred dollars a month, depending on model and streaming. Since you're looking at PLG, we'll provision credits to cover pilot usage.
03:33 Hana: We have a couple of enterprise prospects already asking about SLA. Do you do SLA on hosted?
03:38 Maya: Hosted is best-effort but we do have enterprise SLA options when you move to Dedicated — guaranteed throughput, percentiles, and on-call support. Many customers start hosted, prove the product, then move to Dedicated with an SLA for paying customers.
03:53 Priya: For the pilot we might want to run a latency and cost micro-benchmark against our sample prompts. Is that something Redwood can help with?
03:59 Maya: Absolutely. We can run a benchmark — we typically run a set of 1000 sample prompts at your concurrency and return P95/P99 latencies and cost per token. We can also test model variants and quantization profiles.
04:15 Liam: Great. I'd like to test two things: 1) latency from our EU staging region, 2) token cost with different model sizes.
04:22 Jordan: We can schedule that. Suggest we do a quick smoke run first to validate integration, then the micro-benchmark. If you can share sample prompts and a small traffic replay (like a 1–2 minute sample) that helps.
04:36 Hana: On data retention — do you retain inputs by default for hosted? We have privacy concerns.
04:42 Maya: By default we retain logs for short window for debugging, but you can opt out and we have options to disable retention for enterprise accounts. For Dedicated/Private, you control retention. We'll include the retention policy doc in the follow-up.
04:56 Liam: Any rate limits or throttling we should be aware of during the pilot?
05:01 Jordan: For self-serve hosted accounts we have burst-friendly limits and adjustable quotas. For heavier sustained throughput you'll want Dedicated. We can temporarily increase quotas for your pilot.
05:12 Priya: Do you do streaming websocket for token streaming? We have a UI that benefits from partial token streaming.
05:18 Maya: Yes, streaming is supported both via HTTP chunked and websockets in our SDKs. That reduces perceived latency for the UI.
05:25 Devon: For private on-prem installs, how intrusive is the package? Our infra team wants clarity on network egress, required ports, and if the control plane talks back to Redwood.
05:35 Maya: Private installs can be air-gapped if needed; the default Private control plane is customer-managed inside your VPC with optional telemetry back to Redwood for support. We'll send an architecture diagram and an install checklist.
05:46 Liam: Nice. One of our concerns is model versioning — when we pin a model for the product, do you support canary rollouts and fallbacks?
05:55 Maya: Yes, our Console supports rollouts, A/B tests, automatic fallback policies to compatible model variants if capacity is constrained. That helps with regressing quality if a model update causes issues.
06:07 Jordan: Jumping ahead — we'll provision an initial $5k credit pack to cover the pilot. Is that size OK for your initial scope?
06:15 Liam: That would be fine. Does that include higher-priority support?
06:20 Jordan: Basic support is included; for prioritized SLAs and phone support we can add that as an add-on during Dedicated conversations. For the pilot, we'll include a dedicated onboarding SE window.
06:30 Hana: Could you walk quickly through the exact quickstart steps? Even bullet points.
06:35 Jordan: Sure. 1) Sign up and verify email; 2) create an API key; 3) install Node/Go SDK or use REST; 4) run quickstart script in repo we send; 5) validate first call; 6) request credits and run micro-benchmark. We'll send the repo link and a sample .env and docker compose if you want local emulation.
06:55 Priya: How long to provision the credits?
06:58 Jordan: Within one business day after we confirm account and scope.
07:02 Liam: On the benchmark — what's the turnaround for results?
07:05 Maya: Typically 48–72 hours after we get samples and access to a test workspace. Sometimes faster if it's small.
07:12 Priya: For our compliance team they'll want SOC2 and an illustrations of encryption at rest and in transit. Also need to know where logs are stored and how long.
07:22 Jordan: We'll send SOC2 summary, data retention policy, and KMS notes. For logs we can export to your S3 and retention is configurable.
07:28 Hana: Any exec-level pricing decks or a simple one-pager we can share with prospects?
07:33 Jordan: Yes, we'll include a concise pricing one-pager and an outline of Dedicated pricing so you can show prospects a path from prototype to SLA-backed tenancy.
07:41 Liam: Good. Switching topics — do you have built-in reranking or embeddings endpoints we can use for recommendations? We're evaluating embeddings for semantic search first, then generation for snippets.
07:56 Maya: We support embeddings and reranking. Embeddings endpoint has batch/streaming options; we also provide similarity search guidance. If you want embedding dimensionality vs model tradeoffs we'll recommend models based on retrieval latency and vector store fit.
08:12 Priya: Any notes on GPU/quantization for cost? We might want to test quantized smaller models to save cost.
08:19 Maya: We have quantization recommendations per workload — we can suggest int8/4-bit profiles that preserve quality for most use cases and dramatically cut cost. We'll include model and quantization recommendation doc in the follow-up.
08:33 Liam: Sounds ephemeral — ok, timeline wise we want the demoable prototype in 2 weeks and pilot run over 2–3 weeks after that. Is that realistic?
08:42 Jordan: Yes, totally realistic. Two weeks to a staging demo if you can prioritize the sample prompts and ephemeral staging keys. Then the pilot with credits across 2–3 weeks to validate cost and latency.
09:00 Hana: Great. Any blockers we haven't raised?
09:04 Devon: One small thing — our infra team needs to know if Redwood stores KV caches or prefix caches in a way that could leak PII. We prefer control over the cache or ability to disable it.
09:16 Maya: Caching is configurable and for enterprise/Dedicated you control cache policies. For hosted we have automatic prefix caching but it's adjustable per-route and you can disable caching for sensitive calls.
09:30 Liam: OK. How do we get started — what's the next meeting?
09:34 Jordan: Next meeting let's be a benchmark results review and pilot scoping call — propose 2026-11-30 for the run and 2026-12-02 for review. We'll put calendar invites after this call.
09:44 Hana: Works for us.
09:46 Jordan: Quick recap of next steps — we'll: send SOC2 and security checklist, provision $5k credits, share quickstart repo and Postman collection, run smoke and micro-benchmark, and schedule the results review. Anything to add?
09:59 Liam: That covers it. Thanks.
10:01 Jordan: Thanks all, will follow up with notes and invites.
